stem: When reviewing pretransplant immunizations for an adult transplant candidate, meningococcal vaccination is especially recommended for which groups?

options.text: Military personnel, travelers to high-risk areas, postsplenectomy patients, and college freshmen living on campus
Only candidates who have already received a kidney transplant
Every candidate regardless of risk factors or vocation
Only pediatric candidates younger than 2 years

explanation.rationale_correct: Recommended pretransplant immunizations include meningococcal vaccine especially for military personnel, travelers to high-risk areas, postsplenectomy patients, and college freshmen living on campus.

rationale_incorrect.B: Meningococcal vaccination is emphasized for specific high-risk adult groups rather than only prior kidney recipients.
rationale_incorrect.C: Meningococcal vaccine is highlighted for defined risk groups rather than universal administration to every candidate.
rationale_incorrect.D: The cited meningococcal groups are within adult candidate immunization guidance rather than limited to toddlers.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Immunizations → B. Recommended Pretransplant Immunizations → 1.a.h.

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Immunizations → B.1.a.h. (meningococcal for military, travelers, postsplenectomy, college freshmen); PDF p. 180 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Meningococcal high-risk groups angle distinct from rabies vocation vaccination (cctc-1086) and pneumococcal post-transplant timing (cctc-1048); anchor verified on Cupples p. 180.

stem: A female transplant recipient asks when pregnancy may be considered after transplantation. Which counseling point aligns with standard references?

options.text: Postpone pregnancy until 1 year after transplant when immunosuppressant doses are likely to be lower
Pregnancy should begin immediately after hospital discharge
Pregnancy is permanently contraindicated after every solid-organ transplant
Immunosuppression must be stopped completely before any pregnancy discussion

explanation.rationale_correct: Pregnancy counseling includes discussing timing, medication risks, rejection risk, and physical effects; the recommendation is to postpone pregnancy until 1 year after transplant when immunosuppressant doses are likely to be lower.

rationale_incorrect.B: Early post-transplant recovery is not the recommended time to pursue pregnancy.
rationale_incorrect.C: Pregnancy may be considered with transplant-team and obstetric coordination rather than being universally prohibited.
rationale_incorrect.D: Pregnancy planning involves medication-risk discussion rather than abrupt cessation of all immunosuppression.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → sexual health / pregnancy → l.iii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Recommendation: Postpone pregnancy until 1 year after transplant when immunosuppressant doses are likely to be lower

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → pregnancy counseling → l.iii. (postpone pregnancy until 1 year post-transplant); PDF p. 121 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Post-transplant pregnancy-timing angle distinct from pediatric HPV/hepatitis B sexual-health teaching (cctc-1087); anchor verified on Cupples p. 121.

stem: When teaching a post-transplant recipient about visitor precautions during respiratory infection season, which guidance aligns with standard infection-prevention references?

options.text: Ask visitors who have had recent infections to postpone visiting
Encourage unlimited visitation regardless of active infection symptoms
Visitors with recent infections should visit without any precautions
Recipients should discontinue immunosuppression when visitors are ill

explanation.rationale_correct: Infection-prevention teaching includes avoiding individuals with known infection and asking visitors who have had recent infections to postpone visiting; if contact cannot be avoided, surgical masks may be used.

rationale_incorrect.B: Unrestricted visitation during active infection risk is contrary to standard precautions.
rationale_incorrect.C: Recent infection in visitors warrants postponing visits or using precautions rather than unprotected contact.
rationale_incorrect.D: Immunosuppression is continued as prescribed; visitor precautions address exposure risk.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → infection prevention → ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Avoid individuals with known infection … Ask visitors who have had recent infections to postpone visiting

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).

stem: A coordinator is updating respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) teaching for transplant families. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: RSV is transmitted primarily through large droplets and fomites.
RSV can survive on nonporous surfaces, skin, and gloves for hours.
RSV spreads only through airborne transmission across large distances without close contact.
RSV cannot survive on environmental surfaces.

explanation.rationale_correct: RSV is transmitted primarily through large droplets and fomites, can survive on nonporous surfaces, skin, and gloves for hours, and requires close person-to-person contact or contact with contaminated surfaces. Statements III and IV are false.

rationale_incorrect.B: Statement IV is false because RSV can survive on surfaces for hours.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statements I and II are true; statements III and IV are false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statements III and IV are false.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → RSV → 6.a. Transmission → i.–iii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Primarily through large droplets and fomites … Can survive on surfaces (nonporous), skin, and gloves for hours … Requires close person-to-person contact or contact with contaminated surfaces

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
